fixes.explanation: Close, friend, but that belt is from a different message. Jeremiah buys a linen belt and hides it in a rock, and it ends up ruined (Jeremiah 13:1-7). Here the LORD hands him a cup, and the words are “…this cup of the wine of wrath…” (Jeremiah 25:15). Two different objects, two different messages.

That's it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah to “…make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it.” (Jeremiah 25:15). Later the passage lists them, from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah to the kings of the north (Jeremiah 25:18-26). I think this is one of the heavy parts of the book.

Prophets is a fair guess, since Jeremiah is a prophet himself. But the LORD says “…all the nations to whom I send you…” (Jeremiah 25:15). The word prophets isn't in that verse. Jeremiah is the one the LORD sends with the cup.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says, “So I took the cup from the LORD’s hand…” (Jeremiah 25:17). Then he makes all the nations drink from it, each one to whom the LORD had sent him. I think that was a heavy thing to carry.
I get why you'd think so, since it's a scary cup. But Jeremiah says, “So I took the cup from the LORD’s hand…” (Jeremiah 25:17). He takes it. I think this was a heavy thing to carry.

No passing, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “You most certainly must drink it!” (Jeremiah 25:28). Nobody gets to hand it down the line like a hot tray out of the oven. The word to a nation that refuses is that they must drink.

Waiting isn't mentioned in that verse, friend. If a nation refuses, the LORD of Hosts says, “You most certainly must drink it!” (Jeremiah 25:28). The answer to a refusal is that they must drink it. Hold onto that line.

Nineveh is a name you may know from elsewhere in the Bible, so I see the pull. But it's not named here. The LORD says the disaster begins with “…the city that bears My Name…” (Jeremiah 25:29). The list in this passage starts with Jerusalem and the cities of Judah (Jeremiah 25:18).

Not the beasts, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, “…I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth…” (Jeremiah 25:29). Easy one to slip on, because all the makes you grab the first big group that comes to mind. The animals aren't mentioned in that verse.

Not a song this time, friend. Jeremiah is to say, “The LORD will roar from on high; He will raise His voice from His holy habitation.” (Jeremiah 25:30). The word is roar. I think this is a heavy part of the passage.

Floodgates of the sky are from the story of Noah, whose story has the flood (Genesis 7:11), so it's a good memory. But here the reason is stated plainly: “…because the LORD brings a charge against the nations.” (Jeremiah 25:31). No flood in this verse. It's the charge that makes the tumult.

That's right, baker. The text says, “Flight will evade the shepherds, and escape will elude the leaders of the flock.” (Jeremiah 25:35). The verse before says, “…the days of your slaughter have come…” (Jeremiah 25:34). I think this is one of the heavy parts.

The harvest is a fair guess, since it's about the land. But the verse says, “…the LORD is destroying their pasture.” (Jeremiah 25:36). Harvest is a good word, it's just not the one the text uses. Shepherds and pasture go together like dough and a hot oven, so lean on that pair, baker.
